## Finding a register

A peripheral header can be thousands of lines long: do not read one from the top. Each
starts with a **map**: one line per register, with its offset, its access, its class, its
fields with their bits, and the lines of the file where its class is. From the table
below, open the header of the peripheral, read its map, then only the lines of the
register you need.

The [README of SvdGenerator](https://github.com/Otatiaro/SvdGenerator#the-generated-api)
describes the generated API: names, shared classes, arrays, named values, the vector table,
and what the code refuses to compile.

## Device headers

| Header | Holds |
|---|---|
| [`device.hpp`](device.hpp) | `device_name`, `device_version` and what the source says of the core |
| [`interrupts.hpp`](interrupts.hpp) | `irq_count` and the `IRQn_Type` enumeration |
| [`vectors.hpp`](vectors.hpp) | `vector_table`, the vector table built at compile time, and the `exception` enumeration of the core |
| [`mmio.hpp`](mmio.hpp) | The register building blocks every peripheral header includes (namespace `mmio`); the same for every device |

`mmio.hpp` does not derive from the source file: it is part of SvdGenerator and carries
its own license, MIT, in its header.
